title: Fossils as Evidence
keyIdea: A fossil is the remains or trace of a living thing from long ago, such as a shell, bone, tooth, leaf or footprint, kept in rock. Fossils are clues. What the living thing needed tells you what the place was like: coral means a warm, shallow sea, ferns mean warm, wet land. Rock forms in layers, and lower layers are older, so a cliff can be read from the bottom up like a story. Fossils show where a rock formed, not where it is now: sea shells near the top of Mount Everest are in old seabed rock that was pushed up. Old fossils that differ from living things, like horses with 4 toes, show that life has changed over millions of years.
familyTip: Make a 'cliff' in a clear jar. Pour in a layer of sand, drop in a small shell, then add soil, then rice. Ask which layer went in first and which object is the 'oldest'. Then tip the jar on its side and talk about how real rock can be pushed up or tilted, but the order of the layers still tells the story.

visual.caption: What was this place like when the fossil was alive? Drag each fossil to a box, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: order rock layers by age, match fossils to where they lived, push a seabed up into a mountain, dig up horse feet, then read a cliff.

kid: A fossil is what is left of a living thing from long ago, kept in rock. It can be a shell, a bone, a tooth, a leaf or a footprint. A fossil is a clue. Ask what the living thing needed. Coral only grows in warm, shallow sea. Ferns need warm, wet ground. Woolly mammoths had thick fur for the cold. So a fossil tells you what the place was like back then.
Rock forms in layers. Mud and sand settle, and new layers pile on top. So the lowest layer is the oldest. Read a cliff from the bottom up, and you read the story of that place in order.

Rocks can move. Sea shells are found near the top of Mount Everest. That rock was once the seabed. Over millions of years it was pushed up into a mountain. Fossils show where a rock formed, not where it is now.

Fossils show that life has changed. The oldest horse fossils had 4 toes on each front foot. Later ones had 3. Horses today have 1 toe, a hoof. This change took millions of years and many, many generations.
adult: Ages 8 to 11. NGSS 3-LS4-1 asks pupils to use fossil data as evidence of the living things and places of long ago. In England, Year 6 pupils learn that living things have changed over time. They also learn that fossils tell us about life millions of years ago. The lab uses three kinds of reasoning. What a living thing needed tells you about the place. The order of layers tells you which is older. A series of fossils shows change over time.

Facts used. In layers that have not been tipped, the lower rock is older (Steno's rule of superposition). The top of Everest is limestone about 450 to 470 million years old. It holds fossils of trilobites and other sea animals (Natural History Museum, USGS). India pushing into Asia raised it, starting about 50 million years ago. Wenlock Edge in Shropshire is a fossil coral reef from a warm sea about 430 million years ago. Fossil leaves and tree stumps are found in Antarctica. Early horses such as Eohippus, about 50 million years ago, had 4 toes on each front foot. Mesohippus, about 35 million years ago, had 3. One-toed horses date from about 4 million years ago. The horse family tree branched; the lab shows three points, not a ladder.

Common mistakes. Children often think the top layer is the oldest. They read a fossil as a clue about the place today, not when the rock formed. They explain sea shells on a mountain with a flood. They think an animal changes its own body by using it, in one lifetime, rather than a group changing over many generations. They think every old bone is a dinosaur. In the lab each slip gets a message that names it. The cliff is a simple model: real layers can be folded or tipped, so the challenge says 'neither has been tipped over'.

practice.prompt: A rock has fossils of fish and sea shells in it. What was this place like when the rock formed?
choices: It was under the sea
It was a hot desert
It was a snowy mountain
practice.hint: What do fish and shellfish need to live?
practice.explain: Fish and shellfish need sea water, so the rock formed under the sea, even if it is on land now.

practice.prompt: Mud settles on a lake bed at about {a} mm each year. How many millimetres of mud build up in {b} years?
practice.hint: Multiply the mm for one year by the number of years.
practice.explain: {a} mm × {b} = {=a*b} mm. Slow layers like this, piled over millions of years, become rock.

practice.prompt: A cliff has {n} layers. They are numbered from 1 at the bottom. Which layer number is the youngest?
practice.hint: New layers settle on top of older ones.
practice.explain: The top layer settled last, so layer {n} is the youngest and layer 1 is the oldest.

practice.prompt: Fossil sea shells are found high up on a mountain. What is the best explanation?
choices: The seabed rock was pushed up over millions of years
A big flood carried them up
Shellfish used to live on mountains
practice.hint: Fossils show where the rock formed. Can rock move?
practice.explain: The shells formed in seabed rock. Over millions of years that rock was pushed up, so the shells went up with it.

practice.prompt: The oldest horse fossils have 4 toes on each front foot. What does that show?
choices: Horses have changed over a very long time
Each old horse lost its toes by running
Fossils are not real animals
practice.hint: Could one horse change its own feet during its life?
practice.explain: The change from 4 toes to 1 took millions of years and many generations. One horse cannot change its own toes.

pool.prompt: Which of these is a fossil?
choices: A footprint of a dinosaur kept in rock
A pebble rounded by the sea
A shell from a snail in the garden today
pool.hint: A fossil is the remains or trace of a living thing from long ago, kept in rock.
pool.explain: The footprint is a trace of a living thing from long ago, kept in rock. A pebble was never alive, and today's snail shell is not old.

pool.prompt: Layer X lies under layer Y in a cliff. Neither has been tipped over. Which is older?
choices: Layer X
Layer Y
They are the same age
pool.explain: X settled first and Y piled on top later, so X is older.

pool.prompt: Fossil coral is found in a hill in England. What does it tell you?
choices: The place was once a warm, shallow sea
Coral can grow on dry hills
England is a warm sea today
pool.hint: Think about where coral grows: on land or in the sea?
pool.explain: Coral only grows in warm, shallow sea water. The rock formed in such a sea long ago.

pool.prompt: Fossil tree leaves are found in rock in icy Antarctica. What can you work out?
choices: It was once warm enough for trees
Trees can grow on ice
The leaves fell there last year
pool.hint: Can trees grow on ice? How old are fossils?
pool.explain: Trees need warmer land than Antarctica has today, and fossils are very old. So Antarctica was once warm enough for forests.

pool.prompt: Sand settles on a seabed at about {a} cm every 1,000 years. How thick is the sand after {b},000 years, in cm?
pool.hint: Find how many lots of 1,000 years there are.
pool.explain: {b},000 years is {b} lots of 1,000 years. {b} × {a} cm = {=a*b} cm.

pool.prompt: A rock layer formed {a} million years ago. The layer on top of it formed {b} million years later. How many million years ago did the top layer form?
pool.hint: The top layer is younger, so it formed fewer years ago.
pool.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b}. The top layer formed {=a-b} million years ago, so it is younger than the one below.

pool.prompt: A cliff has coral at the bottom, ferns in the middle and sand dunes at the top. Which story does it tell?
choices: Sea, then swamp forest, then desert
Desert, then swamp forest, then sea
All three at the same time
pool.hint: Read the layers from the bottom up.
pool.explain: The bottom layer is oldest, so first there was a warm sea, then a swamp forest, then a desert.

pool.prompt: A mammoth tooth is found in rock. What was the place like when the mammoth lived?
choices: A cold, icy grassland
A warm, shallow sea
A rainforest
pool.hint: Woolly mammoths had thick fur and ate grass.
pool.explain: Woolly mammoths were built for the cold and ate grass, so the place was a cold grassland in the Ice Age.
